title: Applied Population Dynamics
text:
Course Objectives and Learning Outcomes
This course will present the theory necessary for understanding wildlife population dynamics, and it will explain how to use theory and data to inform management and conservation efforts. By the end of the course, students will be able to: (1) Develop models to forecast the impacts of environmental change and management actions on wildlife populations; (2) Design field studies to collect data on wildlife demographics; (3) Use statistical software to analyze data on wildlife populations; (4) Review scientific literature to support modeling decisions; (5) Present modeling results in a short scientific paper and an oral presentation.

Definitions

title: The BIDE model
text:
Models and science
A model is an abstraction of reality that describes the relationship between two or more variables.

Models help us…

Describe complex natural systems in a manageable way
Formalize and evaluate hypotheses
Predict future outcomes
…all while accounting for uncertainty

title: The BIDE model
text:
The BIDE model
\[N_{t+1} = N_t + B_t + I_t - D_t - E_t\]
\(N_t\): population size (state variable) at time \(t\)
\(B_t\): births
\(I_t\): immigrants
\(D_t\): deaths
\(E_t\): emigrants

title: The BIDE model
text: The BIDE model

title: The BIDE model
text:
The BIDE model
\[N_{t+1} = N_t + B_t + I_t - D_t - E_t\] As written, this model implies the following:

\(B\), \(I\), \(D\), and \(E\) are not rates, they are the number of events at time \(t\).
The model is deterministic, not stochastic
Time is discrete, not continuous


In reality, things are more complicated, and interest lies in understanding the factors influencing each process.

title: The BIDE model
text:
Group exercise


Split into groups of 4–6.
 Come up with a list of at least 5 factors that influence the four demographic variables: B, I, D, and E.

Be prepared to explain which demographic variables are influenced by each factor.

title: WILD 7700 Model
text:
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)


# Create an empty Leslie matrix A
A <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)


years <- 1:50
nyears <- length(years) 

# Vital rates (means and standard deviations for environmental stochasticity)

f3 <- 1.288    # Initial fecundity rate
sd_f3 <- 0.02  # SD for fecundity (environmental stochasticity)
s1 <- 0.36     # Initial survival for age class 1
sd_s1 <- 0.448 # SD for survival of age class 1
s2 <- 0.43     # Initial survival for age class 2
sd_s2 <- 0.448 # SD for survival of age class 2

# Initial population for 3 age classes
n <- matrix(NA, nyears, 3)
n[1,] <- c(4, 4, 7)  # Initial population sizes in year 1

# Logistic growth parameters
rmax <- 0.02  # Maximum growth rate
K <- 25       # Carrying capacity

# Total opulation abundance 
N <- rep(NA, nyears)
N[1] <- sum(n[1,])  # Total population size at time t=1

# For loop
for (t in 2:nyears) {
  
  # Add environmental stochasticity to vital rates
  f3_t <- max(0, rnorm(1, mean = f3, sd = sd_f3))         
  s1_t <- max(0, min(1, rnorm(1, mean = s1, sd = sd_s1)))  
  s2_t <- max(0, min(1, rnorm(1, mean = s2, sd = sd_s2)))  
  
  # Reproduction: New class 1 members produced by class 2 and 3
  if (n[t-1, 2] + n[t-1, 3] > 0) {
    new_class1 <- rpois(1, lambda = f3_t * (n[t-1, 2] + n[t-1, 3]))
  } else {
    new_class1 <- 0
  }
  
  # Deaths of class 1, 2, and 3 
  class1_deaths <- rbinom(1, size = max(0, n[t-1, 1]), prob = 1 - s1_t)
  class2_deaths <- rbinom(1, size = max(0, n[t-1, 2]), prob = 1 - s2_t)
  class3_deaths <- rbinom(1, size = max(0, n[t-1, 3]), prob = 1 - s2_t)
  
  # Update population sizes for the next time step
  n[t, 1] <- new_class1                         # New class 1 born
  n[t, 2] <- max(0, n[t-1, 1] - class1_deaths)  # Surviving class 1 become class 2
  n[t, 3] <- max(0, n[t-1, 2] - class2_deaths + n[t-1, 3] - class3_deaths)  # Surviving class 2 and 3
  
  # Total population size
  N[t] <- sum(n[t, ])  
  
  # Apply logistic growth with density dependence
  ## growth_term <- 1 + rmax * (1 - N[t] / K)
  ## N[t] <- N[t] * growth_term  # Adjust total population size by logistic growth term
  
  ## # Update the population sizes with density dependence
  ## n[t, ] <- pmin(n[t, ], K)  # Ensure population sizes do not exceed carrying capacity
  ## n[t, ] <- pmax(0, n[t, ])  # Ensure no negative population sizes
}

## WITH TRANSLOCATION
# Create an empty Leslie matrix A
A <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)

# Set up years and population array
years <- 1:50
nyears <- length(years) 

# Vital rates (means and standard deviations for environmental stochasticity)
f3 <- 1.288    # Initial fecundity rate
sd_f3 <- 0.02  # SD for fecundity (environmental stochasticity)
s1 <- 0.36     # Initial survival for age class 1
sd_s1 <- 0.448 # SD for survival of age class 1
s2 <- 0.43     # Initial survival for age class 2
sd_s2 <- 0.448 # SD for survival of age class 2

# Initial population for 3 age classes
n <- matrix(NA, nyears, 3)
n[1,] <- c(4, 4, 7)  # Initial population sizes in year 1

# Logistic growth parameters
rmax <- 0.02  # Maximum growth rate
K <- 25       # Carrying capacity

# Population abundance array
N <- numeric(nyears)
N[1] <- sum(n[1,])  # Total population size at time t=1

# Management action parameters
translocation_amount <- 10  # Number of woodrats to translocate

# For loop
for (t in 2:nyears) {
  
  # Add environmental stochasticity to vital rates
  f3_t <- max(0, rnorm(1, mean = f3, sd = sd_f3))
  s1_t <- max(0, min(1, rnorm(1, mean = s1, sd = sd_s1)))  
  s2_t <- max(0, min(1, rnorm(1, mean = s2, sd = sd_s2)))  
  
  # Reproduction: New class 1 members produced by class 2 and 3
  if (n[t-1, 2] + n[t-1, 3] > 0) {
    new_class1 <- rpois(1, lambda = f3_t * (n[t-1, 2] + n[t-1, 3]))
  } else {
    new_class1 <- 0
  }
  
  # Deaths of class 1, 2, and 3 
  class1_deaths <- rbinom(1, size = max(0, n[t-1, 1]), prob = 1 - s1_t)
  class2_deaths <- rbinom(1, size = max(0, n[t-1, 2]), prob = 1 - s2_t)
  class3_deaths <- rbinom(1, size = max(0, n[t-1, 3]), prob = 1 - s2_t)
  
  # Update population sizes for the next time step
  n[t, 1] <- new_class1  # New class1 born 
  n[t, 2] <- max(0, n[t-1, 1] - class1_deaths )  # Surviving class 1 become class 2
  n[t, 3] <- max(0, n[t-1, 2] - class2_deaths + n[t-1, 3] - class3_deaths + translocation_amount) # Surviving class 2 and class 3 plus 10 translocated adults
  
  # Total population size
  N[t] <- sum(n[t, ])  
  
  # Apply logistic growth with density dependence 
  growth_term <- 1 + rmax * (1 - N[t] / K)
  N[t] <- N[t] * growth_term  # Adjust total population size by growth term
  
  # Update the population sizes with density dependence
  n[t, ] <- pmin(n[t, ], K)  # Ensure population sizes do not exceed carrying capacity
  n[t, ] <- pmax(0, n[t, ])  # Ensure no negative population sizes
}
